1878.dq: Crowther 1852 p.5: 'Words taking the middle tone generally carry the accent, as in English, on the first syllable' (word-level remark; the modern sources reached describe lexical tone per syllable/word and state nothing about stress at word or phrase level).
1878.dloc: Crowther 1852: Introductory Remarks (orthography, unnumbered) and section 'ACCENTS', pp. 3-5 (scan page heads 'ACCENTS. 3' / '4 ACCENTS.' / 'SYLLABLES. 5'); Laniran & Clements 2003 sec. 2.1 'Yoruba tonal structure'; Orie 2006 sec. 3.1, p.122.
1878.prule: Lexical three-level tone (H acute, L grave, M unmarked) on every syllable, contrastive on monosyllables (Laniran & Clements 2003; Orie 2006; Crowther 1852). No word-stress rule is stated in any modern description reached; Crowther 1852 says the written accents mark tone ('intonation'), explicitly NOT stress, and adds only an impressionistic remark that all-mid-tone words 'generally carry the accent, as in English, on the first syllable'.
1878.srule: Not mentioned in Crowther 1852 ('Accents', pp. 3-5) or in the modern sources read (Laniran & Clements 2003; Orie 2006; Akinlabi & Liberman 2001; Przezdziecki 2005 p. 104 fn. 1: stress 'is not a distinctive feature in Yorùbá'). Historical only: Bowen 1858 sec. 28, 'a lighter secondary accent usually falls on the second syllable before or after the primary' (impressionistic; not confirmed by any modern description).
1878.quote: [Crowther 1852, Introductory Remarks] Of the accents, none are employed, as in English, merely to mark the stress to be laid on a particular syllable. ... The acute (’) and grave (*) accents are simply marks of intonation— ... i. e. of the rise or fall of the voice—often, as in the Chinese language, ... affecting the signification. ... [p.3, ACCENTS] The Yoruba language is very musical: certain marks to distinguish the tones thus become indispensable. Two accents have therefore been used to point out this distinction, i.e. not to imply that a particular stress is to be laid on the accentuated…
1878.loc: Crowther 1852: Introductory Remarks (orthography, unnumbered) and section 'ACCENTS', pp. 3-5 (scan page heads 'ACCENTS. 3' / '4 ACCENTS.' / 'SYLLABLES. 5'); Laniran & Clements 2003 sec. 2.1 'Yoruba tonal structure'; Orie 2006 sec. 3.1, p.122.
1878.idn: Yoruba; Crowther takes 'the Capital—or Oyó—pronunciation' as the standard (vs. the 'Provincial dialects—the Ibapa and the Ibollo'); Laniran & Clements 2003 and Akinlabi & Liberman 2001: 'standard Yoruba' / 'Standard Yoruba'; Przezdziecki 2005: Standard Yorùbá (SY) plus Àkùré and Mọ̀bà dialects; data: Crowther 1852…
1878.exq_: No stress rule is stated by the modern sources; Crowther's only stress-like remark is itself hedged: 'Words taking the middle tone generally carry the accent ... on the first syllable'.
1878.tone: Three lexically distinctive level tones H/M/L (Laniran & Clements 2003 sec 2.1; Orie 2006 sec 3.1: 'Yoruba has three tones: High (H) rá ‘disappear,’ Low (L) rà ‘buy,’ and Mid (M) ra ‘rub’ (Ward 1952, Bamgboṣe 1966a,b, Awobuluyi 1978).'; Akinlabi & Liberman 2001), plus downstep/terracing at utterance level (Laniran & Clements). Crowther 1852 already states the acute/grave marks are 'simply marks of intonation... affecting the signification' and 'not to imply that a particular stress is to be laid on the accentuated syllable'; H-throughout and L-throughout polysyllables are marked on the first syllable only (an orthographic economy, not a stress claim). a full-text search of the three modern open texts for stress|accent|metrical|foot|prominence returns only 'accent' = tone diacritic and English-L2 stress transfer (Orie: learners 'impose the English stress pattern on words'); none describes Yoruba word stress. The standard reference grammars (Ward 1952, Bamgbose 1966, Awobuluyi 1978) were not reachable open-access.

tn.quote: Yoruba is a tone language with three lexically distinctive tone levels, as illustrated in (1). In our transcriptions, H (high) tones are marked with the acute accent (´), L (low) tones are marked with the grave accent (`), and M (mid) tones are unmarked: lú ‘to mix together,’ ìlú ‘city,’ lu ‘to perforate,’ ìlu ‘perforator,’ lù ‘to beat,’ ìlù ‘drum.’ ... Whenever a H tone syllable and a L tone syllable come into contact (in either order), the tone of the first syllable spreads onto the second to create a contour tone.
tn.cite: Laniran, Yetunde O. & G. N. Clements. 2003. Downstep and high raising: interacting factors in Yoruba tone production. Journal of Phonetics 31: 203-250 (uncorrected proof YJPHO 193); also read: Akinlabi & Liberman 2001, The tonal phonology of Yoruba clitics (sec. 2.1); Orie 2006, L2 Acquisition and Yoruba Tones (sec. 3.1); Crowther 1852, Grammar of the Yoruba Language ('Accents')
tn.note: Three level tones H, M, L; falling/rising contours arise by Tone Spread. Downstep automatic, non-distinctive (F0 study). Akinlabi & Liberman posit a floating subject-marking H. No stress statement. Checked against the source (tone consistency check, 2026-09-23): tone-bearing unit unstated -> syllable (sec. 3.2 'Results', author-proof p. 8; Fig. 1 caption proof p. 9 …); downstep unstated -> yes (Abstract, proof p. 1; end of sec. 5 …).

1879.tone: Kidder 2013 abstract: Yucatec Maya "features both phonemic tonal distinctions and phonemic vowel length"; short vowels "lack any phonemic tonal distinctions". Bennett 2016: "The existence of contrastive tone in Yucatec was firmly established by Pike (1946)... The present consensus... seems to be that Yucatec has the following tonal specifications: a. Short vowels [V]: no tonal specification... b. Long vowels: (i) High tone... (ii) Low tone... c. Rearticulated vowels: high-falling tone". On stress Bennett: Kidder "concludes... that Yucatec has 'no concrete pattern of obligatory stress on the word level'. Gussenhoven & Teeuw (2008) take the anchoring of phrase-level intonational contours in Yucatec as evidence for stress on long vowels and word-initial short vowels, though they concede that stress is 'non-obvious...from a phonetic perspective'".

tn.quote: Vowels in YM are argued to fall into 4 phonemically distinct types of articulation in the YM word, which combine pitch, duration, and laryngealization features, and will be called Short, Low, High and Glottalized. Short vowels are also called Neutral, because they lack a tonal element found in the other vowel types. ... Short vowels are realized with shorter durations than the other three articulation types, and lack any phonemic tonal distinctions. ... Vowels that are marked for either Low or High tone are phonetically longer, and orthographically are written as geminates.
tn.cite: Kidder, Emily. 2013. Prominence in Yucatec Maya: The Role of Stress in Yucatec Maya Words. PhD dissertation, University of Arizona.
tn.locator: sec. 2.5.1.2.1 'Vowel Shapes', pp. 40-41; supporting: ch. 1 p. 13 ('well documented contrast between High and Low tones'), sec. 3.3.3 p. 64, sec. 3.6 p. 73
tn.note: High vs Low tone contrastive on long vowels only; short vowels toneless; glottalized (rearticulated) V'V is a third long nucleus with high pitch and creak. Kidder finds no demonstrable word stress.

1879.cfw: Yucatec is a tone language by every instrumental account (Kügler, Skopeteas & Verhoeven 2007; Sobrino Gómez 2013; Kidder 2013), but whether it also has word stress is openly contested: Bricker, Po'ot Yah & Dzul de Po'ot 1998 put stress on the long vowel or else the final syllable, Gussenhoven & Teeuw 2008 on long syllables and a word-initial short syllable, Andrade 1955 calls accent lexical, Kidder 2013 finds no obligatory word-level stress at all, and DiCanio & Bennett 2018 conclude there is little consensus.

dqtr.text: Burguest & Payne (1991) write "... A very frequent phenomenon that is associated with the level of the phonological word is stress. In fact in many languages stress fulfils the function of demarcating the boundary of phonological words". ... Primary stress falls on the last syllable of the word and secondary [stress] on the first.

1880.dq: Burguest & Payne (1991) escrevem "... Um fenômeno muito freqüente que se associa com o nível da palavra fonológica é o acento. Na verdade em muitas línguas o acento cumpre a frinção de demarcar a fronteira das palavras fonológicas". ... O acento primário recai na última sílaba da palavra e o secundário na primeira.
1880.dloc: Cap. II 'Prosódia', §3 'Acento', §3.1 'Regras Acentuais em Yuhup' and §3.2 'Inventário das Regras Acentuais', pp. 57-60; §2 'Duração' p. 52; Conclusão pp. 120-121; tone: Cap. II §1 'Tom' pp. 31-52.
1880.prule: Predictable: primary stress on the last syllable of the word, secondary stress on the first syllable; affixes are extrametrical (suffixes never stressed) EXCEPT the plural suffix, which takes the final primary stress (e.g. [tih-wah-'r@?@:h] 'os antigos', [m..n-'rw?..:h] 'cestos'); with two suffixes both are extrametrical (['põh-ih-mõh] 'ouvir', [k@e:'ro?-ih-mõh] 'respondeu'). Net: stress = final syllable of (root/stem + plural suffix if present). Vowel lengthening accompanies the stress (duração coincide com o acento de intensidade).
1880.srule: One secondary stress on the first syllable of the word ('o acento primário recai na última sílaba da palavra e o secundário na primeira'), marked in words of three or more syllables ([ˌporegŋˈhɔːh] 'avião', [ˌhɔ̃pˉpɔjhi̠ʔˈmĩː] 'surubim', [ˌtih-wah-ˈræʔæːh] 'os antigos'); disyllables carry only the final primary ([teˈteːj]); non-iterating (no further rhythmic stresses marked in longer words).

II sec.1, pp. 31-52) finds contrastive tone only in a restricted environment (9 minimal pairs, nouns/adjectives; H/L and rising/falling contours measured with CECIL): 'Nos demais ambientes o tom não é contrastivo na língua Yuhup, o que nos leva a concluir que os dados aqui apresentados sejam os resquícios do que foi um língua tonal no passado' (p. 52). Stage B reached a UNAL secondary (Díaz Romero 2009, trabajo de grado co-directed by Ospina Bozzi, p. 8) tabulating three later primaries, all treating tone as distinctive: Lopes y Parker (1999: 330, IJAL 65(3):324-342 'Aspects of Yuhup Phonology'): 'El tono funciona para establecer distinciones de artículos léxicos y de los tiempos verbales. En yuhup, existen dos tonos de registro (alto, bajo)... y dos tonos modulados (ascendente, descendente) distintivos'; Ospina (2002: 52-58): 'El tono es distintivo. Posee dos tonos de registro (alto y bajo). Una unidad portadora de tono... puede tener uno o dos tonos asociados a ella... También, el tono juega un papel importante en la flexión temporal del verbo'; Martins V. (2005: 94-97): 'Fonéticamente, existen 4 tonos... pero solo los dos tonos modulados cumplen función fonológica distintiva de artículos léxicos. tn.quote: A língua Yuhup apresenta em alguns ambientes a oposição significativa entre os tons. 1.1. No primeiro caso temos um número limitado de pares mínimos, constituídos por substantivos e adjetivos, onde o tom é um fator fonêmico de diferenciação lexical. … O percentual de desnível apresentado em cada palavra superior a 6%, demonstra a existência de tons de contorno do tipo baixo/alto e alto/baixo. … Nos demais ambientes o tom não é contrastivo na língua Yuhup, o que nos leva a concluir que os dados aqui apresentados sejam os resquícios do que foi um língua tonal no passado.
tn.translation: The Yuhup language shows in some environments a meaningful opposition between tones. 1.1. In the first case we have a limited number of minimal pairs, made up of nouns and adjectives, where tone is a phonemic factor of lexical differentiation. ... The percentage of pitch offset shown in each word, above 6%, demonstrates the existence of contour tones of the low/high and high/low type. ... In the remaining environments tone is not contrastive in Yuhup, which leads us to conclude that the data presented here are the remnants of what was a tonal language in the past.

1881.prule: Primary stress on the initial syllable of the ROOT (domain of stress = root); non-contrastive, predictable, quantity-insensitive. Because Yuki is almost entirely suffixing and suffixes/enclitics never shift stress, the surface pattern is word-initial primary stress in the typical word. Off-initial cases are morphologically defined: the small set of body-part prefixes (mi-/me-, na-, ną-/nam-, hą-/ham-) and kin-possessive prefixes are unstressed (stress on root-initial syllable = word syllable 2); reduplicant is unstressed (stress on syllable 2, Schlichter 1978:16); lexicalized compounds take primary stress on the initial syllable of the second (head) element with secondary on the first element; some disyllabic verb roots (e.g. wilíṭ- 'pass') carry stress on their non-initial syllable, analysed as fossilized prefixation/compounding.
1881.srule: Secondary stress on the penultimate (second) syllable of trisyllabic words with monosyllabic roots (wą́.kì.wič); on the prefix in prefixed nouns and verbs (ną̀.ná.kuč); on the initial syllable of the first element of lexicalized compounds (ˀùk-hóṭ 'ocean', mìlon-títam 'elk'). Placement in words of four or more syllables and in words with disyllabic roots not determined (too few tokens in the Logan recording).

tn.quote: Tone. The function of tone in Djerma is a subject in need of more study. Djerma words exist having two or more different meanings, which appear to be distinguished, in isolation, only by a difference in tone. However, when these same words are uttered within the context of a sentence, the tonal distinction is blurred, and it is often difficult to detect the difference in tone heard previously when the word was uttered in isolation. 1886.prule: Final syllable of the phonological word (omega) is the most prominent syllable; 'no contrastive stress'. Omega = lexical root plus any prefixes (1-3 moras); enclitics and each member of a compound are separate phonological words, so 'root-final' = omega-final. Prominence is realized primarily as longer vowel duration (intensity is tone-dependent) and as licensing of maximal contrast (vowel length, nasality, /o/, tone patterns restricted to/greatest at the final syllable). quantity-insensitive: position licenses length, not the reverse. Author explicitly rejects a rhythmic-stress analysis.
1886.srule: None: no secondary or rhythmic stress; each phonological word (1-3 moras) has one prominence peak, its final syllable. Campbell explicitly rejects a rhythmic-stress reading of alternating longer/louder syllables in connected speech ('an example like this might make it appear as if the language had rhythmic stress manifested as duration. However, this is not what is going on'): they are the final-syllable prominences of successive phonological words (compound verb = two omegas, then two disyllabic words).

tn.quote: Zenzontepec Chatino has two tones: high tone V́, and mid tone V̄. The tone bearing unit (TBU) is the mora, but not every mora carries lexical tone. Therefore, there is in effect a three-way tonal contrast on the mora: high tone V́, mid tone V̄, and no tone V. … there are nine logically possible tone patterns for a bimoraic form … However, only five of them are found on phonological words that are not stems inflected for second person singular person: ØØ, ØM, MH, HØ, and HM. These will be referred to as the five basic tone patterns.
tn.cite: Campbell, Eric William. 2014. Aspects of the phonology and morphology of Zenzontepec Chatino, a Zapotecan language of Oaxaca, Mexico. PhD dissertation, The University of Texas at Austin (August 2014).
tn.note: Two level tones, high and mid, contrasting with toneless moras (TBU = mora); five basic word tone patterns; H spreads and downsteps a following H or M; at most one H per word; no contrastive stress.

1889.heavy: McGarrity (rendering J. Payne 1990): 'Syllables with long vowels (indicated in the data with a double vowel) and diphthongs are considered to be heavy and always attract stress (except in word final position). While, in general, closed syllables are considered to be light, a syllable that is closed with a nasal consonant and that contains the short high front vowel [i] in the nucleus is considered to be heavier than an open syllable containing short [i]. Finally, the syllables /tsi/ and /sji/... are considered to be extralight; they are never stressed.' Scale (31): CVV(N) > CV(N), CiN > Ci > tsi, sji. Rasin: 'CVV(C) syllables are heavy and CV(C) are light'. StressTyp2: 'In feet, Heavy=VV'.
1889.dflt: All-light words (McGarrity ex. 32a, data from J. Payne 1990): (há.ka) 'here', (no.pí)to, (ka.máN)ta.ke, (no.tòN)(ka.méN)to, (no.kó)(wa.wé)ta.ka, (ha.mà)(naN.tà)(ke.né)ro, (pa.mè)(na.kò)(weN.tá)ke.ro: iambs from the left, final syllable extrametrical, light penult in clash destressed, primary on the rightmost surviving foot head -> initial syllable in disyllables, 2nd syllable in 3- and 4-syllable words, penult in odd-parity words of 3+ syllables, antepenult in even-parity words of 4+ (secondaries on the even-numbered syllables to the left); overridable by the Ci primary-shift and the /tsi/,/sji/ avoidance ([pì.sji.tá.tsi.ri] 'broom').
1889.prule: Left-to-right iambs, feet (LL), (LH) or (H); CVV (long vowel or diphthong) heavy and always stressed except word-finally; CV(N) light (CiN ranks above Ci; /tsi/, /sji/ extralight, never stressed); final syllable extrametrical and never stressed even if heavy; clash resolved by deleting the stress on the rightmost of two adjacent stressed lights at the end of the parsing string (adjacent heavies may both keep stress). Primary stress = head of the rightmost foot (so it lands on the penult, antepenult or preantepenult), except that when that head is a light Ci syllable and the head of the preceding foot has a, e or o, primary shifts to the preceding foot (McGarrity 34b [(máa)(ki.ri)]ti, ñàa.wyàa[(ta.wá)(ka.ri)]ri). Pre-heavy destressing: obligatory for a stressed light Ci before a stressed heavy, optional for CV(N)/CiN (Rasin 80a/b a.tì.ri.pà.yée.ni ~ a.tì.ri.pa.yée.ni); a further Ci-destressing is obligatory before Ca (o.pi.ná.ta) and optional before Ce, Co, Ci (i.kí.te.ti ~ i.ki.té.ti); Rasin also mentions rapid-speech destressing.
1889.srule: All non-primary stresses assigned by the same rules are secondary: every second syllable counted from the word start (2nd, 4th...; the count restarts after a heavy), every non-final heavy CVV syllable (even adjacent ones), never the final syllable; light Ci and extralight tsi/shi syllables lose or shift their stress as in the primary rule; in rapid speech light-syllable stresses drop. No secondary stress after the primary ('Despues del acento primario, no hay acento secundario', Payne 1989:42; Payne 1990:198 leaves the post-primary foot unmarked, while Hayes 1995:295, per McGarrity 2003 fn.18, assumes post-tonic secondaries). Secondary stress is not sonority-sensitive (McGarrity 2003 sec. 4.3.2.3).

morph.elicq: No statement of how the stress data were obtained. The rules are framed by speech style: 'En palabras más largas (de cinco sílabas o más), el estilo del habla determina si una sílaba débil debe ser acentuada o no. En el habla lenta y cuidadosa las sílabas débiles pasan a ser normales, pero en el habla rápida las sílabas débiles no son acentuadas' (SLP28 pp.39-40, with paired Lento/Rápido examples); and Lección 14 p.298 'Repaso del acento': 'Las palabras que se ven en las columnas A y B han sido extraídas de los diálogos y los textos. La columna B lleva la acentuación que corresponde a la pronunciación correcta y cuidadosa.'
morph.stmt: Predominantly suffixing: the only pre-root material is one person prefix (subject on verbs, possessor on nouns: 'el sujeto de todos los verbos está en el verbo mismo bajo la forma de un prefijo pronominal', SLP28 p.44) plus the future nasal prefix m-/n- ('Los prefijos de tiempo', p.89), while Cuadro 15.1 'El verbo' (pp.320-321) lists two prefix columns (PREFIJO, FUTURO) against eleven ordered suffix columns after the stem (Modal-1, Modal-2, Direccional, Aspecto, Tiempo, Persona, Persona, Plural, Relativo, Adverbial, Modo: 'Los sufijos del verbo ashéninca siguen un orden estricto', p.319); in the 80 text tokens there are 48 prefix morphs (30 syllables) versus 134 suffix morphs…

1890.dq: The phonological word is defined as a unit with one primary stress. In Abau, primary stress is associated with the first syllable of the phonological word. (Lock 2011:22) ... The most salient stress within the phrase is not necessarily on the first word of the phrase, but is rather on the head of phrase. (Lock 2007:41)

1890.prule: fixed-initial: primary stress on the first syllable of the phonological word (highest pitch and intensity), pitch falling syllable by syllable to the last syllable
1890.srule: None within ordinary words: after the initial primary stress 'each syllable following will be lower in pitch and volume than the preceding syllable' (Lock 2007:22; Lock 2011:22 defines the phonological word as 'a unit with one primary stress', lowest pitch on the last syllable). Non-primary peaks are reported only in reduplications joined by a linker (third syllable of lowp-a-lowp 'all' higher than the second, lower than the first; Lock 2007:22) and on the noun of an interrogative+noun NP stress unit ('the noun following has secondary stress', Lock 2011:279).

1891.dloc: Chapter II (Fonetika), section 'Udarenie', pp. 62-67. quote and domain passage (dq): p. 64. Affix classes and exceptions: p. 65, continuing at the top of p. 66 (p. 67, read this stage). Minimal-pair list pp. 63-64; compound and syntactic stress pp. 66-67 (scan).
1891.prule: Free, contrastive (lexically distinctive) dynamic word stress with no fixed position: stress may fall on the first, second, third etc. syllable and is in a huge number of cases the only difference between words (а́ла 'eye' vs ала́ 'dog', а́сра 'beat' vs асра́ 'weave', ауаса́ 'sheep' vs ауа́са 'so'). Placement is a lexical property of stems and affixes: stems with a closed monosyllabic base or a polysyllabic base with non-final stress keep fixed stress under affixation; stems with an open (CV) monosyllabic base have mobile stress, shifting forward onto stress-accepting affixes or backward off them; affixes divide into stress-accepting (most conjugational morphemes) and never-stressed (instrumental -la, adverbial -ta, privative -da, most derivational formants, interrogative -ma in Tapanta proper).
1891.srule: Exists occasionally, no placement rule: a word normally carries one stress; long predicative (polysynthetic verb) complexes may carry two stresses, the second weakened (уыгIасзы́нхахд 'you stayed for me'), and rarely an optional weak stress appears on another vowel of a bound-morpheme combination beside the main stress (па̀дыркIы́лыйд). No rhythmic/alternating secondary stress described (Lomtatidze 2006: 112 likewise: one stress prevails, sometimes a weaker co-stress).

1891.tone: Genko p. 63 (scan): stress is expiratory; 'С ударением в абазинском языке нормально не связано ни сколько-нибудь заметное повышение тона ударяемого гласного, ни удлинение его' - no noticeable pitch rise or lengthening, which makes Abaza stress harder to hear than Russian or Abkhaz stress. Dybo, Nikolaev & Starostin 1978 (Estonian Papers in Phonetics, pp. 17-18) claim two tones, high and low, on the stressed syllable of Tapanta; a minority instrumental hypothesis not adopted by the descriptive grammars, and Genko explicitly denies pitch involvement. Not a tone language.

1892.prule: No positional rule. The only first-hand observer gives no rule from which position could be computed.

1893.heavy: Not defined in Sec. 3.3 itself. All four shift examples in (37) have a closed (CVC) final syllable after an open (CV) penult; (32)c a.ˈuk 'go.2' (V.VC) and (30)c nutˈnɨt 'manioc beer (masato)' (CVC.CVC) on the same page also carry final stress, so heavy = syllable with a coda (CVC or VC). Sec. 3.2 (p. 11) lists the attested syllable types as V, CV, CVC (all positions) and VC (initial/final) and refers to 'the prosodic behavior of heavy syllables (see discussion below) in four-syllable forms'. No vowel-length contrast is attested; the authors speculate that the (38) exceptions might be relics of a lost contrastive vowel length.
1893.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable (head of a right-aligned disyllabic trochee) when the last two syllables are of equal (light) weight; the rightmost foot becomes iambic, i.e. primary stress falls on the final syllable, when the final syllable is heavier (closed, CVC) than the penult (aˈʃap, tuˈkut, ɾajwãˈʔãk, a.kɾeˈwak).
1893.srule: Secondary stress on every second syllable to the left of the primary stress (iterative right-aligned disyllabic trochees, no degenerate feet): on the pre-antepenult in four- and five-syllable words ((ˌta.ha)(ˈru.ʔu) 'garden', (ˌi.sa)(ˈra.wi) 'woodpecker', as(ˌlan.ta)(ˈni.a), sa(ˌmak.ta)(ˈni.a) 'young woman'); two- and three-syllable words have a single stress and a leftover initial syllable is unstressed (wi(ˈʃa.la)).

1895.tone: Nevin 1998 p.60: every syllable is H (acute) or L (unmarked); falling tone analyzed as HL over a vowel cluster; ch.6 'Reduplication' (pp.127-129) treats verb roots as H and instrumental prefixes as L. On stress the whole 182-page work says only: lax vowel allophones occur only in unstressed syllables and may be tensed if stressed in careful citation (p.58); a glottal stop is optionally inserted before a stressed onsetless syllable, and 'Stress and pitch are independent, as is shown in (93)' where qá as has L on the stressed syllable (p.94); 'reduced stress' on the auxiliary duji causes final-syllable devoicing (ch.1, p.41 of PDF); geminate onset 'to a stressed syllable' (ch.1). No section on stress; a full-text search of stress/accent/prominence/foot/rhythm/metrical finds no placement rule; sec.4.1 'positional prominence' is Beckman's onset/coda notion. de Angulo & Freeland 1930 p.80: two main tones high/low plus descending and ascending; 'the pitch-tone of every syllable is absolutely set' (interrogative section); their 'stress accent' remark is about Atsugewi and Shasta, not Achumawi. Uldall 1933: two tonemes (high level, low level), no rising/falling; a tendency among younger speakers to put final syllables on low or falling tone; two chronemes; no stress statement.

1896.prule: One primary accent per phonological word (higher pitch, longer duration, greater amplitude on one vowel); its position is contrastive and NOT predictable from syllable count, weight or any metrical principle, and varies within and across speakers. Tendencies only: nouns accent a root vowel; a limited set of suffixes attract accent; nominal suffixes/clitics often shift accent one vowel rightward (júmi 'water' vs jumí=nʲ 'water=OBJ'); verbs accent root or certain suffixes; compounds, noun phrases and reduplications take a single accent, usually on the last vowel of the first member (hápa 'red brocket' vs hapá_jãwãã 'cougar'; t͡ʃirít͡ʃiri). Fast 1975 (Peruvian Achual, DEL 20 p. 9): 'El acento constituye otro contraste fonémico' with minimal pairs núnka 'tierra' vs nunká 'en la tierra', héa 'casa' vs heá 'en la casa'.
1896.srule: None (one prominence per word): 'all Shiwiar words exhibit a single prosodic prominence... but its placement is not predictable and it varies from word to word'; sec. 5.3.3 describes no secondary or rhythmic stress.
1896.quote: All Shiwiar words exhibit a prosodic prominence which I have labelled as accent in this work. tn.translation: On the tonal level, one easily demonstrates the opposition of two level tones, H and L (B), and two contour ('modulated') tones, HL and LH. A QUANTIFICATION rule accounts for the downdrift characteristic of the language; everywhere except before pause, the falling contours HL are reduced to H by a PONCTUALISATION (levelling) rule. The language makes use of floating tones, written (H) and (B), at both the lexical and the grammatical level. ... LH has properties distinct from the sequence L - H (and moreover comparable to those of HL, since both contour tones lower any following H by downstep).

[...] Распределение словесного ударения в словах, произнесенных во фразе, отличается от ударения в изолированных словах.» (word stress in isolated words explicitly contrasted with phrasal stress and with 'logical' stress)

1904.prule: Main stress bound to the first syllable of the word, quantity-insensitive and non-contrastive ('mechanical'); Kert 1975 states it for all Saami dialects with Akkala/Babino explicitly enumerated (p. 207) and again in §14 for isolated words (p. 218); Zajkov 1987, the only Akkala-specific description, presupposes 'stress resting on the first syllable' in a diachronic remark on apocope (p. 76) while declaring the accentual-rhythmic structure of the word outside its scope (p. 73).
1904.srule: Secondary stress on the following odd-numbered syllables (3rd, 5th, 7th), never on the word-final syllable; all stresses rhythmic ('mechanical') and non-distinctive. Stated as common to all Saami dialects with Akkala/Babino enumerated; the Akkala-specific monograph (Zajkov 1987) does not treat secondary stress.
1904.quote: Zajkov 1987, 76: «Отпадение конечных гласных в саамском, как и в других финно-угорских языках, можно объяснить, видимо, тем, что ударение, покоящееся на первом слоге, привело сначала к редуцированию конечного гласного, а затем к полному его исчезновению.» ibid. 73: «Наименее исследованной, по крайней мере, на материале кольско-саамских диалектов, остается акцентно-ритмическая структура слова.» Kert 1975, 207: «Общность фонетической структуры слова в диалектах саамского языка проявляется также в главном ударении, которое падает на первый слог, и в последующих второстепенных ударениях, падающих…
